title: Number systems, codes and complements
subtitle: Hardware has two states, so every number, letter and sign is a pattern of 0s and 1s. Learn the patterns.

digital.title: Why binary
digital.body: An analog signal varies continuously and picks up noise; a digital signal is interpreted as only two levels (low = 0, high = 1) with a wide margin between them, so small noise is ignored and copies are exact. A bit is one binary digit; 8 bits make a byte. n bits give 2ⁿ patterns.
digital.steps: How many different values can 10 bits represent? Each bit doubles the count.

conv.title: Converting between bases
conv.body: In base r each place has weight rᵏ. To convert to binary, divide by 2 repeatedly and read remainders upward; from binary, add the weights of the 1s. Octal and hex group bits in 3s and 4s, so conversion is just regrouping. For decimal 25: binary 11001, octal 31, hex 19.
conv.steps: 25 ÷ 2 = 12 r 1; 12 ÷ 2 = 6 r 0; 6 ÷ 2 = 3 r 0; 3 ÷ 2 = 1 r 1; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r 1. Read the remainders upward.

bcd.title: BCD, excess-3 and Gray
bcd.body: BCD writes each decimal digit in 4 bits: 25 → 0010 0101. Excess-3 adds 3 to each digit (0101 1000), which is self-complementing. Gray code changes only one bit between neighbouring values (10101 for 25) — ideal for position encoders because no glitch between steps can show a wrong value.

neg.title: Signed numbers
neg.body: Three schemes: sign–magnitude (top bit is the sign), 1’s complement (invert all bits), 2’s complement (invert, then add 1). 2’s complement wins: one zero, and addition just works. For −25 in 8 bits: sign–magnitude 10011001, 1’s 11100110, 2’s 11100111. A 4-bit word covers −8 … +7.

add.title: Adding and overflow
add.body: In 2’s complement, add as usual and discard the carry out. Overflow occurs when two numbers of the same sign give a result of the opposite sign (equivalently the carry into and out of the sign bit differ). In 4 bits, 5 + 4 = 9 does not fit in −8…+7: 0101 + 0100 = 1001, which reads as −7.
add.steps: 0101 (+5) + 0100 (+4). Result 1001 is negative although both inputs were positive: overflow.

ascii.title: Characters and parity
ascii.body: ASCII assigns 7-bit codes to characters: ‘A’ = 65 = 1000001₂, ‘a’ = 97. Unicode extends this to all scripts (UTF-8). A parity bit makes the count of 1s even (or odd) so a single flipped bit is detected — though not corrected.
ascii.steps: Even parity for ‘A’ = 1000001 (two 1s). Already even, so the parity bit is 0.
